text:
7.2 Figure 1.2: Subnational Agricultural Capital Valuation & Subcounty Spatial Apportionment
Section in Platform: Section 1.2  |  Target Identifier: fig_1_2  |  Output Type: Chart

Policy / Scientific Question: What agricultural and livestock capital is exposed to climate extremes in the county, how much of it is standing herd wealth as opposed to annual harvest and offtake value, and how is it distributed across the county’s constituencies?


7.2.1 Scientific Purpose & Context
Climate risk screening needs a value at risk. A drought that kills a fifth of a county’s cattle and a drought that cuts its maize harvest by a fifth are different events: the first destroys capital that takes years of breeding to rebuild, the second destroys one year’s income. Global gridded value-of-production surfaces, including the Atlas-wide MapSPAM crop and Gridded Livestock of the World (GLW4) livestock layers expressed in constant 2015 international dollars, conflate these two things. They value livestock by annual output (meat offtake and milk), so a pastoral county’s wealth is represented by a small flow number while the herd itself, the asset that drought actually erodes, does not appear. In the earliest version of this figure that approach valued Marsabit’s cattle at about 31 million US dollars and omitted camels entirely, which no pastoral planner would recognise.
Figure 1.2 therefore rebuilds the county portfolio from Kenya’s statutory statistics and separates two quantities explicitly. Standing stock is the replacement value of the live herd: head counts from the 2019 Kenya Population and Housing Census and the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) National Agricultural Production Report (NAPR), valued at county sale prices with a capital-share adjustment for herd structure. Annual flow is the value of what the county produces in a year: crop harvests at farm-gate prices, livestock offtake and milk, and official livestock products (eggs, honey, hides, poultry meat). Both are reported in constant 2021 Kenyan shillings with a fixed 2021 conversion to US dollars, so that changes between years reflect physical quantities, not price inflation or exchange-rate movements. A portfolio chart shows the composition by commodity, and a constituency view apportions every county total across the 290 parliamentary constituencies (IEBC sub-counties) with mass-preserving spatial weights.
The output is a screening estimate of exposure, built for comparing counties and sub-counties and for sizing contingency planning. It is published under Beta review governance: livestock prices in the arid and semi-arid counties are annual medians from National Drought Management Authority (NDMA) county drought early warning bulletins used under research fair dealing while formal licensing is sought, so the asset tables are shown for expert review, are not released as open data and carry no bulk download.


7.2.2 Mathematical Formulation & Algorithmic Approach
Baseline Reference Period: Valuation base year 2021 (constant 2021 KES; USD at the 2021 annual average rate); crops 2019 to 2024, livestock and products 2021
Tier 1, quantities. Crop production by county and year comes from the KNBS NAPR 2023/24 and 2024/25 editions (deterministic PDF table extraction with additivity gates), supplemented by Agriculture and Food Authority (AFA) county returns for paddy rice and by Horticultural Crops Directorate county values for vegetables and fruits in 2021. Livestock head counts by county and species (cattle, camels, goats, sheep, donkeys, pigs, poultry) come from the 2019 Kenya Population and Housing Census (KPHC) Volume IV household livestock tables and the NAPR livestock population tables for 2021; the dairy share of the cattle herd is taken from the KPHC exotic-dairy count and, in highland counties only, scaled so that the national dairy herd matches the NAPR total. Livestock product quantities (milk, eggs, honey, hides, poultry meat) are the KNBS 2021 county figures.
Tier 2, prices. The base year is 2021 and all prices are 2021 Kenyan shillings (KES) at farm-gate or primary-market level. Crop prices follow a documented preference order: AFA Yearbook 2021 farm-gate prices first (coffee on a cherry-equivalent basis, tea at the Kenya Tea Development Agency green-leaf rate), then KNBS Economic Survey Table 7.4 average gross prices to farmers, then MapSPAM 2020 FAOSTAT-derived producer prices as the last resort. Live-animal sale prices in the 23 arid and semi-arid counties are 2019 to 2021 annual medians of the NDMA county drought early warning bulletins; elsewhere they are 2021 Kenya Agricultural Market Information System (KAMIS) medians and literature values for dairy cattle, donkeys, pigs and poultry. Milk is priced at county milk prices. Every parameter and price carries source identifiers resolvable in a sha256-verified source registry, and the build fails if any identifier is missing.
Tier 3, livestock parameters. Standing stock for cattle, goats and sheep is head count times a capital share of 0.75 times the sale price; the capital share reflects that a herd’s immatures and breeding females are not all saleable at the quoted price of a mature animal. Camels are valued at the NDMA sale price times an empirical herd-structure ratio (1.39 in Marsabit, 0.99 in Isiolo, 1.17 nationally). Annual flow is head count times an annual offtake rate times sale price (cattle 0.12 in arid and semi-arid zones and 0.08 in the highlands; camels 0.04; goats 0.16; sheep 0.14) plus milk litres times milk price, where cattle milk is dairy head times 800 L per head per year plus non-dairy head times a zone coefficient (55 L in arid, 100 L in semi-arid and highland zones), and camel milk is 180 L per head per year. Zone coefficients derive from the Behnke and Muthami (2011) audit of Kenyan livestock contribution to GDP, cross-checked against the primary sources, with goat milk from Field (1985). Counties are assigned to arid, semi-arid or highland zones from the 2015 Ending Drought Emergencies county list.
Tier 4, currency. Flows and stocks are converted to US dollars at the KNBS Economic Survey 2021 annual average of 109.65 KES per USD. The rate is fixed to the base year so that the dollar series is a constant-price series; a current rate is available only as an explicit user override. The legacy constant 2015 international dollar layers from MapSPAM and GLW4 are retained for comparison with the Atlas-wide exposure product but do not enter the county totals.
Tier 5, subcounty apportionment. Each county total for a commodity is distributed across its IEBC parliamentary constituencies in proportion to a spatial prior specific to that commodity. For crops and horticulture the prior is MapSPAM 2020 v1r2 physical area for the matching crop (or crop group), summed from the 5 arc-minute grid cells whose centroids fall inside each constituency. For livestock and livestock products the prior is the KPHC 2019 household livestock count for the species (or species group) by constituency, obtained by crosswalking census sub-counties to IEBC constituencies with the GLW4 density surface as the reference layer. Where a prior sums to zero within a county (12 percent of crop rows, under 1 percent of livestock rows) the constituency land-area share is used instead and the row is flagged as a fallback. Shares are gated to sum to one within each county and commodity to within 1e-12, and the apportioned values are gated to re-aggregate exactly to the county totals.

7.2.2.1 Methodological Rationale
Why constant base-year prices. The purpose of the figure is to expose physical production and herd capital to climate hazard, so the valuation must not move when prices move. Kenyan farm-gate prices and the shilling both shifted sharply over the data window (the shilling went from 109.65 per US dollar in 2021 to 139.85 in 2023, and KNBS revised the 2022 maize price upward by 35 percent between editions). Valuing every year’s quantities at the same 2021 prices and the same 2021 exchange rate means that a change in the series is a change in tonnes or head, which is what a drought or flood alters. The 2021 base year was chosen because it is the latest year for which KNBS county livestock populations, the Economic Survey price tables, the AFA yearbook and the NDMA bulletin price medians all overlap.
Why stock and flow are separated. Drought mortality and distress sales erode the herd, which is a capital stock; a poor harvest erodes one year’s output, which is a flow. Reporting only flow, as the gridded international-dollar layers do, makes pastoral counties look poor and under-states what a multi-season drought puts at risk; reporting only stock makes crop counties look poor and ignores the income shock. The capital-share parameter corrects a second conflation: multiplying every head by the sale price of a mature animal overstates herd value because a herd is mostly females and immatures, so the 0.75 share, derived from empirical Kenyan herd demographic structures, brings the stock value to a replacement basis. Camels receive a species-specific ratio because their herd structure and price structure differ from those of cattle and small stock.
Why mass-preserving dasymetric apportionment. County totals are statutory; constituency totals are not published. The honest way to produce a sub-county figure is to keep the county total fixed and distribute it with the best available spatial evidence of where the commodity is, which is the pycnophylactic (mass-preserving) property of dasymetric mapping. The priors are chosen to be commodity-specific so that maize follows maize area and camels follow camel counts, not population or land area. MapSPAM and GLW4 enter here only as spatial shape, never as level, so their known biases in absolute value (which motivated the rebuild) do not propagate into the totals.
Why Beta review governance. The NDMA bulletin prices are copyright NDMA with no open licence; they are used as derived annual medians under research fair dealing while permission is sought. Until that permission exists the assets cannot be redistributed, so the module carries a Beta Review Edition banner, provides no bulk download, and is excluded from the open Atlas data store and the Comprehensive Data Hub. The values are screening estimates for exposure comparison and contingency sizing; they are not calibrated for use as the basis of fiscal transfers, insurance payouts or compensation without further validation against county-level market and herd surveys.
Governing Mathematical Formulations:
County crop flow (gross value of production at constant 2021 farm-gate prices). Q is county production in tonnes from KNBS NAPR (plus AFA rice and HCD horticulture); the price for each crop is taken from the first available source in the preference order.
\[
F^{\text{crop}}_{c,y} = \sum_{i=1}^{I} Q_{c,i,y}\; P_{i}^{2021}, \qquad P_i^{2021} \in \{\text{AFA farm-gate} \succ \text{KNBS ES Table 7.4} \succ \text{FAOSTAT via MapSPAM}\}
\]
County livestock standing stock (herd replacement capital). H is head count (KPHC 2019 and NAPR 2021), kappa is the capital share or camel herd-structure ratio, and the sale price is the NDMA 2019 to 2021 median in ASAL counties or the KAMIS 2021 median elsewhere.
\[
S_{c} = \sum_{j} H_{c,j}\; \kappa_j\; P^{\text{sale}}_{c,j}, \qquad \kappa_j = \begin{cases} 0.75 & j \in \{\text{cattle}, \text{goats}, \text{sheep}\} \\ \rho^{\text{camel}}_{c} & j = \text{camels} \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\]
County livestock annual flow (offtake plus milk). r is the annual offtake rate by species and zone z(c); M is milk litres with the dairy herd at 800 L per head and the non-dairy herd at the zone coefficient (55 L arid, 100 L semi-arid and highland); camel milk is 180 L per head.
\[
F^{\text{live}}_{c} = \sum_{j} H_{c,j}\; r_{j,z(c)}\; P^{\text{sale}}_{c,j} \;+\; \sum_{j} M_{c,j}\; P^{\text{milk}}_{c}, \qquad M_{c,\text{cattle}} = H^{\text{dairy}}_{c}\cdot 800 + \left(H_{c,\text{cattle}} - H^{\text{dairy}}_{c}\right)\cdot m_{z(c)}
\]
County livestock product flow and portfolio totals. Products (eggs, honey, hides, poultry meat) use KNBS 2021 county quantities at the KNBS 2021 national unit value; the dollar conversion is fixed at the 2021 annual average rate.
\[
F^{\text{prod}}_{c} = \sum_{g} Q_{c,g}\; \bar{P}^{\text{KE}}_{g}, \qquad F_c = F^{\text{crop}}_{c} + F^{\text{live}}_{c} + F^{\text{prod}}_{c}, \qquad V^{\text{USD}} = \frac{V^{\text{KES}}}{109.65}
\]
Subcounty apportionment shares (mass-preserving dasymetric weights). Weights are commodity-specific; where the prior sums to zero within a county the constituency land-area share is substituted and the row flagged as a fallback.
\[
w_{sc,i} = \frac{A_{sc,i}}{\sum_{k \in c} A_{k,i}} \ \ (\text{crops: MapSPAM physical area}), \qquad w_{sc,j} = \frac{H^{\text{KPHC}}_{sc,j}}{\sum_{k \in c} H^{\text{KPHC}}_{k,j}} \ \ (\text{livestock: census head}), \qquad \sum_{sc \in c} w_{sc,\cdot} = 1
\]
Apportioned constituency values and county-sum identity. The build gates that apportioned values re-aggregate exactly to the statutory county totals.
\[
S_{sc} = \sum_{j} w_{sc,j}\, S_{c,j}, \qquad F_{sc} = \sum_{i} w_{sc,i}\, F_{c,i} + \sum_{j} w_{sc,j}\, F_{c,j}, \qquad \sum_{sc \in c} S_{sc} = S_c, \quad \sum_{sc \in c} F_{sc} = F_c
\]

7.2.4 Methodological Assumptions & Analytical Limitations

Beta Review Edition governance: livestock prices for the 23 ASAL counties derive from NDMA county drought early warning bulletins used under research fair dealing pending formal NDMA licensing. The asset tables are provided for expert review only, carry no bulk download, and are not published to the open Atlas data store or the Comprehensive Data Hub.
The values are macro-level exposure screening estimates. They are suitable for comparing counties and constituencies and for sizing contingency plans; they are not calibrated for direct use in fiscal transfers, index insurance payouts or compensation schedules without validation against county market and herd surveys.
Livestock head counts are 2019 census household counts and 2021 NAPR populations. Pastoral herds are mobile and partly enumerated away from the household, and herd sizes changed substantially through the 2020 to 2023 drought; the 2021 baseline predates most of that mortality.
The capital share (0.75), camel herd-structure ratios, offtake rates and milk coefficients are zone-level parameters from audited literature, not county surveys. Each carries a documented range in the parameter file; the point estimates are used in the figure and the ranges are not propagated as uncertainty bands.
Milk coefficients rest on Behnke and Muthami (2011) field audits and on Field (1985) for small stock, with the dairy-herd scaling applied in highland counties only; dry-county dairy herds are deliberately left unscaled because national scaling inflated them 1.3 to 13 times.
Crops are valued for 2019 to 2024 but livestock and products for 2021 only, so the portfolio is a 2021 snapshot and the crop time series should not be read as a trend in total assets.
Crop prices mix three sources with different bases (farm-gate, gross price to farmers, FAOSTAT producer price). Horticulture enters as county-reported values rather than as quantity times price.
MapSPAM 2020 physical area is itself a modelled allocation of national and sub-national statistics to a 10 km grid, so crop apportionment inherits its allocation errors; in heterogeneous pastoral ecotones the cropland prior and the census livestock prior both carry classification error, and 12 percent of crop rows fall back to land-area shares.
The KPHC 2019 census sub-counties do not coincide with IEBC constituencies; the crosswalk introduces boundary error in counties where the two geographies diverge.
Fisheries, forestry, draught power, manure and the non-market services of livestock are outside the valuation; the flow is a gross value, not value added, and input costs are not deducted.
County aggregations rely on official polygon boundaries (IEBC constituencies via UN OCHA COD-AB); historical boundary changes are not back-cast.

text:
7.3 Figure 4.1: Dual-Season Ocean Drivers vs. Agricultural & Livestock Output
Section in Platform: Section 4  |  Target Identifier: fig_3_1  |  Output Type: Chart

Policy / Scientific Question: In the years covered by official county statistics, how did crop production, livestock numbers and livestock product value move relative to their typical level, and what were the two rainy seasons and the ocean drivers doing in the seasons that fed each year?


7.3.1 Scientific Purpose & Context
Annual agricultural output in Kenya is fed by two rainy seasons, and harvests lag the rains that grew them. Figure 4.1 lines up the official county statistics from the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) National Agricultural Production Report (NAPR) with the seasons that fed each year, so a planner can see whether a weak year followed a failed season, a double failure, or neither.
The upper panel plots the selected crops, livestock species or livestock products for the county as an index relative to each item’s median over the surveyed years (100 = typical), or as raw values. The lower strips show, for each year, the seasonal rainfall anomaly in percent of the 1991–2020 mean and the seasonal ocean driver values (Relative Oceanic Niño Index, Dipole Mode Index and the Western-V index) against their phase thresholds, with an optional vegetation (NDVI) overlay. For crops the year is a harvest year, and it is paired with the preceding Short Rains (OND of the previous calendar year) and the concurrent Long Rains (MAM). Livestock and product years are paired with the same calendar year’s MAM and OND, with lagged values available in the table view.
The figure is a descriptive, record-linking tool. The KNBS county series currently span only 2019 to 2024 for crops and 2021 to 2023 for livestock and products, so it supports reading individual recent years against their seasons, for example the 2020 to 2022 multi-season drought, rather than estimating how output responds to ocean drivers in general. Longer-run crop responses are examined with HarvestStat county series elsewhere in Section 4.


7.3.2 Mathematical Formulation & Algorithmic Approach
Baseline Reference Period: Output indexed to the median of the surveyed years; rainfall anomalies against the 1991–2020 WMO standard normal
Output series. For the selected county the figure assembles three groups from the KNBS NAPR extractions: crop production in tonnes (with paddy rice from Agriculture and Food Authority county returns), livestock head counts by species, and livestock product value in Kenyan shillings, excluding values flagged as suspect during extraction. The user chooses a group and up to a few items (by default the two leading food crops). Only positive values are plotted. The years shown are the years with data for the selected items: currently 2019 to 2024 for crops and 2021 to 2023 for livestock and products.
Median index. Each item’s typical level is the median of its positive values over the surveyed years. In the default view each value is plotted as an index, 100 times the value divided by that median, so that items with very different units share one axis. The table view reports the percentage deviation from the median and flags deviations of at least +15 percent and at most −20 percent. No trend is fitted or removed.
Season pairing. For crops, year Y is a harvest year paired with OND of year Y−1 and MAM of year Y, following the national convention that Short Rains crops are harvested in the following calendar year. For livestock and products, year Y is paired with MAM and OND of the same year, and the table adds the preceding seasons as lagged columns.
Seasonal climate strips. Rainfall is shown as the percentage anomaly of the county-mean CHIRPS v3 seasonal total against its 1991–2020 mean; SPEI-3 is available as an alternative. The ocean drivers are the CPC RONI for the season (falling back to a seasonal mean of monthly values when the seasonal record is missing), the mean of the available monthly HadISST DMI values over the season (ERSST where HadISST is missing), and the mean of the standardized Western-V index over March to May. Each driver is drawn against its phase thresholds: ±0.5 °C for RONI, ±0.4 °C for DMI and ±0.5 standard deviations for Western-V. The bars are coloured by season, not by phase.

7.3.2.1 Methodological Rationale
Why a median index rather than a detrended anomaly. Detrending needs a series long enough to estimate a trend separately from the shocks of interest. The KNBS county series are four to six years long, and a linear trend fitted to them would absorb a drought year as readily as a real trend in area or productivity. The median of the surveyed years is the most robust typical level available for so short a record: it is not pulled by one extreme year, and it makes items in tonnes, head and shillings comparable on one axis. Long-run teleconnection effects on yield are better examined with the multi-decadal HarvestStat county series shown elsewhere in Section 4, which are long enough to separate trend from shocks.
Why explicit season pairing. Placing an annual harvest beside same-year seasonal shading invites a misreading, because the Short Rains of year Y are harvested in year Y+1. The figure therefore pairs each crop harvest year with the preceding OND and the concurrent MAM, labels the axis as harvest year, and draws the two seasons as separate bars, so the lag is part of the visual grammar rather than a footnote. Livestock numbers and products are census and survey-year quantities with no single harvest date, so they are paired with the same year’s seasons and the lagged seasons are reported alongside.
Why raw driver thresholds here. The strips are a reading aid placed against the physical index values that county planners encounter in bulletins and outlooks, so they use the conventional raw thresholds for each index rather than the standardized classes used for the contingency analysis in Figure 3.2.
Governing Mathematical Formulations:
Median index of output. V is production (t), head count or product value (KSh) for item j; the set of years is the item’s surveyed years in the county.
\[
I_{j,Y} = 100\,\frac{V_{j,Y}}{\tilde{V}_j}, \qquad \tilde{V}_j = \operatorname{median}\{V_{j,y} : y \in \mathcal{Y}_j,\ V_{j,y} > 0\}
\]
Deviation from the median (table view). Asymmetric flag thresholds highlight shortfalls more readily than surpluses.
\[
\delta_{j,Y} = 100\,\frac{V_{j,Y} - \tilde{V}_j}{\tilde{V}_j}, \qquad \text{flag: } \delta \ge +15\%\ \text{or}\ \delta \le -20\%
\]
Season pairing by output type. Crop years are harvest years; Short Rains crops are harvested in the following calendar year.
\[
\text{crops: } Y \leftrightarrow \left(\text{OND}_{Y-1},\ \text{MAM}_{Y}\right), \qquad \text{livestock and products: } Y \leftrightarrow \left(\text{MAM}_{Y},\ \text{OND}_{Y}\right)\ \text{with lagged } \left(\text{MAM}_{Y-1},\ \text{OND}_{Y-1}\right)
\]
Seasonal rainfall anomaly. County-mean CHIRPS v3 seasonal totals.
\[
A^{\%}_{s,y} = 100\,\frac{R_{s,y} - \bar{R}_{s,1991\text{--}2020}}{\bar{R}_{s,1991\text{--}2020}}, \qquad s \in \{\text{MAM}, \text{OND}\}
\]
Driver phase reference lines. Seasonal means of the indices drawn against conventional raw thresholds.
\[
\text{RONI} \gtrless \pm 0.5^\circ\text{C}, \qquad \text{DMI} \gtrless \pm 0.4^\circ\text{C}, \qquad \text{Western-V} \gtrless \pm 0.5\,\sigma
\]

7.3.4 Methodological Assumptions & Analytical Limitations

The record is very short. Crops have at most six surveyed years and livestock and products three, so the figure cannot estimate a response to ocean drivers; it only places individual years beside their seasons. No correlation, regression or significance test is computed.
The median of four to six years is itself uncertain and is pulled toward whatever conditions dominated the surveyed years; for 2019 to 2024 that period includes the 2020 to 2022 drought, so the “typical” level may be lower than a longer-run normal.
Output is not detrended, and changes in planted area, herd management or KNBS survey coverage between editions are not separated from weather effects.
Crop production mixes MAM-grown and OND-grown harvests in one annual figure, so a single harvest year reflects both seasons in unknown proportions that vary by county and crop.
Livestock head counts and product values are stock and survey quantities whose response to drought is lagged and cumulative; pairing them with same-year seasons understates the effect of earlier seasons, which the lagged table columns only partly address.
Values flagged as suspect in the NAPR product tables are excluded, and blanks are not treated as zeros, so some items have gaps.
The optional NDVI overlay is drawn only for surveyed years, so the preceding Short Rains value is often unavailable for the first year shown.
Driver strips use seasonal means of whatever monthly values are available, without a completeness check, and the Western-V index is defined only for MAM.
County aggregations rely on official polygon boundaries from the UN OCHA Common Operational Datasets (COD-AB).

section: 8.1 enso-driver-indices: Ocean Climate Teleconnection Drivers (Pacific RONI, Indian Ocean DMI & Western-V)
text:
8.1 enso-driver-indices: Ocean Climate Teleconnection Drivers (Pacific RONI, Indian Ocean DMI & Western-V)
Category: Climate  |  Publishing State: authored  |  License: Open Data

8.1.1 Summary
Harmonised multi-decadal monthly and seasonal time series of primary equatorial ocean-atmosphere climate teleconnection drivers governing Kenyan rainfall: NOAA CPC Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI) for Pacific ENSO state; NOAA CPC / HadISST Dipole Mode Index (DMI) for Indian Ocean Dipole state; and Funk et al. Western-V SST index for MAM Long Rains teleconnections. Standardised and compiled into analysis-ready parquet tables (1950 to present).

Temporal Coverage: 1950-01 to present (open-ended)
Spatial Resolution: global-oceans, equatorial-pacific, indian-ocean



8.1.2 Data Producers & Custodians

NOAA Climate Prediction Center - https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/
Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (Peter Steward)



8.1.3 Scientific Caveats & Guidance

[!WARNING] Attribution: “Data provided by NOAA Climate Prediction Center (CPC) and compiled for the African Agriculture Adaptation Atlas (AAAA).” RELATIVE OCEANIC NINO INDEX (RONI) OVER RAW NINO 3.4. CPC computes RONI by subtracting the tropical-mean (20S-20N) SST anomaly from the Nino 3.4 anomaly. This detrending removes secular tropical ocean warming (~+0.6 degC since 1950) that otherwise causes historical cool baselines to register as artificial permanent El Nino conditions. Always use RONI for multi-decadal analogue selection. INDIAN OCEAN DIPOLE (IOD) DOMINANCE IN SHORT RAINS. The DMI is the primary physical forcing of Kenyan rainfall variability during the October-December (OND) Short Rains. Warm ENSO and positive IOD co-occur frequently but can decouple; off-diagonal states (El Nino + negative IOD) produce subdued anomalies. SEASONAL ASYMMETRY AND LONG RAINS (MAM) DECOUPLING. Pacific ENSO indices exhibit weak correlation with Kenyan rainfall during the March-May (MAM) Long Rains (r ~ 0.08). The Western-V index captures western Pacific warm pool gradients that govern convective subsidence over the Horn of Africa, providing independent predictive skill where ENSO fails. Z-SCORE STANDARDIZATION REQUIREMENT. Pacific SST anomalies (~0.5-2.5 degC) and regional rainfall anomalies exhibit a 10.6:1 variance distortion ratio. Multi-driver analogue selection must use z-score standardisation across all driver dimensions to ensure equal physical weighting.

8.2 africa-precipitation-monthly-seasonal: Monthly and Seasonal Precipitation from CHIRPS v3 (Africa)
Category: Climate  |  Publishing State: authored  |  License: Open Data

8.2.1 Summary
Total precipitation (PTOT) aggregated from CHIRPS v3.0 and delivered as per-pixel monthly Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs and per-year rolling 3-month (seasonal) sums over Africa, 1981 to present. This is the rainfall backbone of the KE-ENSO Explorer’s seasonal/ENSO analysis: the twelve seasonal windows (JFM, FMA, …, DJF) are the tri-month sums the notebook compares against ENSO phase and against the drought (SPEI), vegetation (NDVI) and flood layers. A derived aggregation product, not a redistribution of the CHIRPS daily archive.

Temporal Coverage: 1981-01 to present (open-ended)
Spatial Resolution: africa — 0.05 deg (~5.5 km, CHIRPS native)



8.2.2 Data Producers & Custodians

Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (Peter Steward)
Climate Hazards Center, UC Santa Barbara - https://www.chc.ucsb.edu/data/chirps



8.2.3 Scientific Caveats & Guidance

[!WARNING] Source CHIRPS is public domain (“no restrictions on use”); these reprocessed COGs are released CC-BY-4.0 with attribution to the Climate Hazards Center, UC Santa Barbara. Seasonal windows are labelled by the calendar year in which the window ends (DJF_2020 = Dec 2019 to Feb 2020). Edge windows that the record cannot cover in full are absent (NDJ and DJF 1981; windows ending after the latest monthly file), so not every season x year combination of the template exists.

8.4 eastafrica-flood-jrc: JRC / GloFAS Return-Period River Flood Hazard (Global)
Category: Satellite  |  Publishing State: authored  |  License: Open Data

8.4.1 Summary
Modelled global riverine flood hazard from the JRC / GloFAS Global Flood Maps (CEMS-GLOFAS v2.1.2): inundation depth for seven return periods, 10 to 500 years, at 3 arc-seconds, as a static baseline climatology. Published as Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs with internal overviews on Source Cooperative, which is the canonical read location. The Adaptation Atlas additionally holds a provisional Kenya crop of the same data. Within the KE-ENSO Explorer this is the MODELLED flood-prone baseline complementing the OBSERVED Copernicus GFM extent (record kenya-flood-gfm): JRC answers “how flood-prone at magnitude X”, GFM answers “where and when it actually flooded”.

Temporal Coverage: None
Spatial Resolution: world, kenya — 3 arc-seconds (~90 m)



8.4.2 Data Producers & Custodians

Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (Peter Steward)
Source Cooperative / Radiant Earth Foundation - https://source.coop/nlebovits/jrc-glofas
European Commission Joint Research Centre (JRC) - https://data.jrc.ec.europa.eu/



8.4.3 Scientific Caveats & Guidance

[!WARNING] FEDERATED TO THE CLOUD-OPTIMIZED UPSTREAM (2026-09-18, following review on cdh-catalog#32). The full global product is already published as COGs with internal overviews under CC-BY-4.0 on Source Cooperative, at the same seven return periods and the same 3 arc-second resolution as the Atlas crop. The canonical asset in this record is therefore the global collection, not our subset. The Kenya crop is retained as a provisional second asset because the KE-ENSO Explorer currently reads it, but it carries no information the global collection lacks and the performance argument for keeping it is untested. Measuring that is the open task; retiring the duplicate is the likely outcome. Static modelled hazard (return-period depths); not an observed time series and not scenario-projected, so no temporal coverage is declared. Pair with the GFM observed extent for the “modelled vs observed” flood story.

section: 8.5 kenya-flood-gfm: Kenya Observed Flood Extent (Copernicus GFM, Sentinel-1)
text:
8.5 kenya-flood-gfm: Kenya Observed Flood Extent (Copernicus GFM, Sentinel-1)
Category: Satellite  |  Publishing State: authored  |  License: Open Data

8.5.1 Summary
Observed flood extent for Kenya from the Copernicus Emergency Management Service Global Flood Monitoring (GFM) product, which classifies flooding from every Sentinel-1 SAR acquisition (ensemble of the DLR, TU Wien and LIST algorithms; permanent and reference water excluded). Delivered as ~111 m aggregates built directly from the 20 m SAR tiles: a monthly flood-occurrence layer with its valid-observation count, a rolling 3-month (seasonal) layer aligned to the KE-ENSO Explorer precipitation seasons, and a full-record history (occurrence frequency and ever-flooded footprint), 2018 to present. Replaces the MODIS Global Flood Database (ended 2018) with a cloud-penetrating, continuously updated SAR record. The 20 m per-acquisition archive is not materialised here (16,000+ acquisitions); it can be re-pulled from the EODC STAC on demand.

Temporal Coverage: 2018-01 to present (open-ended)
Spatial Resolution: kenya — 0.001 deg (~111 m); aggregated from 20 m Sentinel-1 tiles (a coarse pixel is flooded if any 20 m sub-pixel flooded)



8.5.2 Data Producers & Custodians

Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (Peter Steward)
Copernicus Emergency Management Service (CEMS) - https://global-flood.emergency.copernicus.eu/



8.5.3 Scientific Caveats & Guidance

[!WARNING] Attribution required: “Contains modified Copernicus Emergency Management Service information [year]”. Pixel coding of the flooded layers: 0 = not flooded, 1 = flooded, 255 = not observed (SAR gap or excluded) - 255 is absence of observation, NOT dry; the nobs layer gives the count of valid observations so no-flood is distinguishable from no-observation. Seasonal windows are named by the initials of their months and labelled by the year of their FIRST month (DJF_2018 = Dec 2018 to Feb 2019), so NDJ and DJF exist for 2018 to 2024 only. This differs from the CHIRPS seasonal record (africa-precipitation-monthly-seasonal), which labels NDJ and DJF by the year the window ends; align on those two windows with care. A ~7-year record measures recent observed flood occurrence, not return-period magnitude.

text:
8.7 eastafrica-wrsi-fews: FEWS NET Water Requirement Satisfaction Index, Cropland and Rangeland (Kenya)
Category: Satellite  |  Publishing State: authored  |  License: Open Data

8.7.1 Summary
End-of-season Water Requirement Satisfaction Index (WRSI) for cropland (maize) and rangeland growing seasons from USGS FEWS NET, for the long rains (MAM) and short rains (OND) of every year from 2003, cropped to Kenya and written as Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs. WRSI is the ratio of seasonal water supplied to crop or pasture water demand (0 to 100 percent); low values flag agricultural water deficit. The crop and rangeland monitoring layer of the KE-ENSO Explorer, on the same CHIRPS v3 precipitation backbone as the rainfall and SPEI layers.

Temporal Coverage: 2003 to present (open-ended)
Spatial Resolution: kenya — 0.1 deg (~11 km, FEWS NET WRSI grid)



8.7.2 Data Producers & Custodians

Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (Peter Steward)
USGS FEWS NET - https://earlywarning.usgs.gov/fews



8.7.3 Scientific Caveats & Guidance

[!WARNING] Cropland and rangeland use different water-demand parameterisations and growing-season definitions (FEWS NET region codes / end-of-season dekads), so the two products are not interchangeable. The {crop} x {season} cells map to FEWS NET East Africa region codes as follows (FEWS NET zip-product instructions, Table 1, 2025-02-03): rangeland OND = e1 (Sep-Jan), rangeland MAM = e2 (Feb-Jul), cropland OND = et (maize, Oct-Feb), cropland MAM = ee (maize, Mar-Nov). Not every season x year combination of the template exists: the most recent season is only published once FEWS NET releases its end-of-season product. PROVENANCE: objects published between 2026-08-18 and 2026-09-20 had the cropland and rangeland labels swapped (e1/e2 served as cropland, ek/et as rangeland); every object was replaced in place on 2026-09-20 and copies fetched before that date should be discarded.

text:
8.8 kenya-flood-exposure-intersect: Kenya Flood x Exposure, Per-Sub-County Tables
Category: Satellite  |  Publishing State: authored  |  License: Open Data

8.8.1 Summary
Pre-computed flood x exposure statistics for Kenya’s 290 IEBC sub-counties (admin 2), as three small Parquet tables the KE-ENSO Explorer reads directly (DuckDB-WASM) instead of intersecting heavy rasters and vectors in the browser. Two hazard products - Copernicus GFM observed flood (per season x year, 2018 to 2025) and JRC modelled return-period flood hazard - are each crossed with population (WorldPop constrained 100 m grid, levelled to the official KNBS county totals), classified roads and the electricity transmission grid (length exposed) and health and school facilities (count exposed); a third table holds the per-sub-county denominators. Tables carry no geometry: join on adm2_pcode to the boundary record kenya-admin-codab.

Temporal Coverage: 2018 to 2025
Spatial Resolution: kenya — IEBC sub-counties (290 admin-2 units)



8.8.2 Data Producers & Custodians

Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (Peter Steward)



8.8.3 Scientific Caveats & Guidance

[!WARNING] Derived aggregate statistics; no input geometry is redistributed. Please attribute the inputs: Copernicus GFM and JRC Global Flood Maps (Copernicus / European Commission), WorldPop constrained population (CC-BY-4.0), OpenStreetMap roads and HOTOSM facilities ((c) OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL), KPLC grid (CC0-1.0, energydata.info), IEBC COD-AB boundaries (OCHA, CC-BY-3.0-IGO). In the GFM table, observed_pct is the SAR-observed share of the sub-county in that season: low values mean sparse observation, not absence of flooding. Road and grid kilometres are cell-resolution approximations (in-cell line length within flooded cells). Every table also carries adm1_pcode, adm1_name and adm2_name label columns. POPULATION METHOD (issue #28), stated in full. Headcounts are NOT raw gridded pixel sums. Every published sub-county population is built as three explicit factors, each published as its own column:


[!WARNING] pop_adm2 = pop_adm2_grid x pop_scale_census x pop_growth_county


[!WARNING] (1) pop_adm2_grid - the 100 m gridded pixel sum, which supplies the SHARE of the county’s people


[!WARNING] living in that sub-county, and nothing else.


[!WARNING] (2) pop_scale_census = census county total / gridded county total - replaces the LEVEL of the


[!WARNING] gridded surface with the enumerated KNBS 2019 census, county by county. The gridded surfaces


[!WARNING] run about 17 per cent above the census (WorldPop constrained ~55.2 M, GRID3 ~55.9 M, census


[!WARNING] 47,564,296), so this factor is ~0.855 nationally but spans 0.324-1.394 across individual


[!WARNING] counties (measured on the published grid, 2026-09-17): WorldPop exceeds the census by up to


[!WARNING] threefold in some counties and falls below it in others. Any aggregate therefore moves by a


[!WARNING] weighted mix of county factors, not by the national one - flood-exposed population sits mostly


[!WARNING] in low-factor counties, so the GFM exposed total fell about 35 per cent where the national


[!WARNING] denominator fell 14 per cent. No time component.


[!WARNING] (3) pop_growth_county = target county total / census county total - the county’s proportional


[!WARNING] CHANGE OVER TIME, from the KNBS Vol XVI projections (record


[!WARNING] kenya-population-knbs-projections). Exactly 1.0 when the denominator is the census itself.


[!WARNING] County is the only level where any of this is defensible: COD-AB adm2 is 290 IEBC constituencies while the census reports 345 KNBS sub-counties, and only 183 names match (record kenya-population-knbs-census); KNBS does not project below county at all. FIXED-SHARE ASSUMPTION. Each sub-county’s share of its county is held constant at the gridded 2020 distribution, so every sub-county in a county moves by exactly that county’s percentage change. Sub-county-specific growth is NOT represented: a fast-urbanising sub-county and a depopulating one in the same county grow at the same rate here. Growth does vary between counties - the 2025 factors span 1.03 to 1.15 - but not within one. YEAR MATCHING (the published default from 2026-09-17). The GFM table records OBSERVED floods and carries a year, so a single fixed denominator is wrong in one direction or the other: the 2019 census undercounts a 2024 flood by roughly 9 per cent, and a 2025 projection overcounts a 2018 one by a similar margin. Each GFM row is therefore levelled against ITS OWN year’s county population, and pop_year records which year was used. Years the KNBS projections cover (2020 onward) use them; 2018 and 2019 fall back to the enumerated census, because nothing official projects backwards from the 2020 base and inventing a figure would be worse than stating the fallback. Consequence for consumers: pop_source VARIES BY ROW in the GFM table - “knbs-census-2019” for 2018-2019 and “knbs-projection-” thereafter - so do not read one value and assume it applies to the file. The JRC table is a return-period hazard with no event year, and the totals table is a static denominator, so both take a single stated reference year (pop_year, same on every row). [!WARNING] county-growth-from- - pop_growth_county = projection(year) / projection(base year,


[!WARNING] 2020). The enumerated census remains the level and KNBS supplies only the shape of change;


[!WARNING] national 2025 lands near 51.96 M because the ~2.6 per cent step KNBS puts between census night


[!WARNING] (August 2019) and its own 2020 base is deliberately not imported.


[!WARNING] county-level - pop_growth_county = projection(year) / census(2019), so the county total IS the


[!WARNING] published official projection and national 2025 is 53,330,964 - the figure a Kenyan


[!WARNING] counterpart would quote - at the cost of superseding the census anchor with the KNBS base-level


[!WARNING] revision.

Nothing is discarded: the raw gridded figures remain in pop_exposed_grid and pop_total_grid. pop_pct is identical under every option - the factors cancel.

[!WARNING] LICENCE EVIDENCE. Attribution is given as a courtesy though CC0 does not require it. The supporting evidence gathered earlier still stands: Evidence for the licence, recorded because knbs.or.ke itself carries no terms page (the terms-and-conditions URL 404s and the footer asserts “All Rights Reserved”), which is misleading: (1) KNBS operates an Open License Agreement covering its Open Data Platform, granting a worldwide, royalty-free, non-exclusive licence to use, copy, modify, publish, adapt, distribute and create derivative works for commercial and non-commercial purposes, subject to attribution. (2) KNBS’s own account on the Humanitarian Data Exchange published the SAME sub-county table used here - “Distribution of Population by Sex, Number of Households, Land Area, Population Density and Sub County” - under Public Domain / No restrictions (https://data.humdata.org/dataset/kenya-population-per-county-from-census-report-2019). (3) The same census figures are redistributed by UNFPA under CC-BY-3.0-IGO (HDX cod-ps-ken). Required attribution, carried by any product derived from this record: “This product was adapted from the Statistical Office of Kenya’s information, which is licensed under the KNBS Open License Agreement.”


[!WARNING] ADMIN LEVELS DIFFER BY LEVEL. County joins one-for-one with IEBC COD-AB (47 units, adm1_pcode). Sub-county does NOT: COD-AB adm2 is 290 IEBC constituencies while the census reports 345 KNBS sub-county rows (a different universe - constituency splits such as Embakasi East/West/Central against sub-county Embakasi, plus 12 forest and national-park units such as Aberdare Forest and Mt Elgon Forest). Normalised in-county name matching resolves 183 of the 290 COD-AB units, so the adm2 table is published in the KNBS universe, name-keyed, with adm2_pcode_codab filled only where a name matches exactly one COD-AB unit inside the same county and codab_match recording how each row resolved. Use county totals plus a gridded within-county share for any adm2 denominator; do not join this table to COD-AB sub-counties on name. Male + Female (47,562,772) falls 1,524 short of the published Total because KNBS suppresses the intersex count below national level; the residual is carried as pop_intersex. The age-and-sex table comes from HDX cod-ps-ken (UNFPA, CC-BY-3.0-IGO), which redistributes the same census (Volume III) with adm1 p-codes attached. DO NOT SWITCH THE SOURCE TO THE HDX COPY of the sub-county table, despite its cleaner licence status: that copy is defective. It carries 346 rows to this source’s 345 because the Tharaka-Nithi COUNTY total (393,177) appears as if it were a sub-county, inflating the national figure to 47,957,473 against the published 47,564,296. This ingest uses the knbs.or.ke workbook, which reconciles exactly. (It also spells Kutulo as “Kotulo”; same value, harmless.)

section: 8.10 kenya-population-knbs-projections: KNBS Official Population Projections by County, 2020-2045 (Kenya)
text:
8.10 kenya-population-knbs-projections: KNBS Official Population Projections by County, 2020-2045 (Kenya)
Category: Demographics  |  Publishing State: authored  |  License: Open Data

8.10.1 Summary
Kenya’s official cohort-component population projections, from the 2019 KPHC Analytical Report on Population Projections (Volume XVI, KNBS 2022), tabulated from the report’s Appendix 5 as county x year x 5-year age group x sex, keyed on IEBC COD-AB adm1_pcode. National trajectory 48.82 M (2020), 53.33 M (2025), 57.81 M (2030), 62.16 M (2035), 66.31 M (2040), 70.18 M (2045). Lets forward-framed flood and drought exposure use a population denominator for the year in question instead of a 2020 surface read as current.

Temporal Coverage: 2020 to 2045
Spatial Resolution: kenya — counties (47 admin-1 units)



8.10.2 Data Producers & Custodians

Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (Peter Steward)
Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) - https://www.knbs.or.ke/



8.10.3 Scientific Caveats & Guidance

[!WARNING] MIXED-STATUS RECORD - READ BEFORE REUSE (decision 2026-09-18). The source documents are KNBS publications, linked here and not hosted by the Atlas. Three DERIVED parquet tables were published to digital-atlas BEFORE the licence was correctly established; they reproduce KNBS figures, so they are NOT open data. They are documented here deliberately: leaving a public object undocumented is worse than describing its true status. They must not be treated as open data, and this record must NOT be submitted to cdh-catalog, until written permission exists from KNBS (info@knbs.or.ke / directorgeneral@knbs.or.ke). Permission request is deferred as of 2026-09-18, so this state persists by decision, not by oversight. HOW THE ATLAS USES THIS WITHOUT REDISTRIBUTING IT. The exposure chain applies projections as a dimensionless growth ratio on a census anchor, never as absolute published values: R/observational/_population_helpers.R, POP_METHOD=county-growth (the default at 7_zonal_exposure.R:138 and 7b_relevel_exposure_pop.R:64) computes projection_county(year) / projection_county(2020) and multiplies the CC0 census count by it, so no published artifact reproduces a KNBS projection. The alternative POP_METHOD=county-level reproduces the official county total exactly and must NOT be used for anything published. SOURCING - CORRECTED 2026-10-07. An earlier version of this note claimed the ratios are read from the Summary Report rather than Volume XVI. That was WRONG: it recorded an intention from the 2026-09-18 decision that was never implemented. python/ingest_population_knbs_projections.py downloads exactly one PDF, Volume XVI (PDF_URL, one urlretrieve_checked call), and the Summary Report URL appears nowhere in python/ or R/. The published tables are their own evidence - they carry 2020-2035 annually plus 2040 and 2045, while the Summary Report carries only 2020-2025, 2030, 2035, 2040 and 2045, so 2026-2029 and 2031-2034 can only have come from Volume XVI. The ratios therefore derive from the rights-reserved document, and the ratio method alone is what keeps published artifacts clear of KNBS figures. Switching the source is not a one-line change: the live reference year is 2026, which the Summary Report does not contain, so it would mean constraining POP_REF_YEAR to covered years - moving the national denominator from 52,837,534 (2026) to 51,961,873 (2025). Tracked on issue #33.


[!WARNING] LICENCE - CORRECTED 2026-09-18, READ BEFORE REUSE OR REDISTRIBUTION. This record previously claimed the KNBS Open License Agreement. That was WRONG. Volume XVI was read directly on 2026-09-18 and its copyright page states: “(c) 2022 Kenya National Bureau of Statistics. All rights reserved. No part of this publication may be reproduced, distributed, or transmitted in any form or by any means … without the prior written permission of the Bureau.” The KNBS Open License Agreement is scoped to data published on the KNBS Open Data Platform and does not reach a PDF published on knbs.or.ke, and a search of HDX on 2026-09-18 found NO licensed mirror of these projections anywhere - the UNFPA COD-PS product (cod-ps-ken, CC-BY-3.0-IGO) carries the 2019 census only and contains no projections, so there is no openly licensed substitute. CONSEQUENCE. Extracting these figures for analysis is ordinary research use. REDISTRIBUTING them, including as the derived parquet files this record points at, needs written permission from KNBS (info@knbs.or.ke / directorgeneral@knbs.or.ke, the addresses given in the report). Until that permission exists this record must NOT be submitted to cdh-catalog, and the published derivatives should be treated as pending clearance rather than as open data. Tracked in hazards_prototype issue 33. This constraint does NOT apply to the census counts - record kenya-population-knbs-census is CC0-1.0, released without restriction by KNBS’s own HDX account.


[!WARNING] LICENCE EVIDENCE. Weaker footing than the census record, and the difference is worth stating. KNBS’s Open License Agreement grants worldwide, royalty-free, non-exclusive rights to reuse, adapt, redistribute and create derivative works with attribution - but it is scoped to data published on the KNBS Open Data Platform, and Volume XVI is a PDF hosted on knbs.or.ke. Unlike the 2019 census tables, no licensed mirror of these projections exists anywhere (searched HDX, open.africa and the Kenya data portal, 2026-09-17): UNFPA’s COD-PS covers the census, not Volume XVI. What is published here is a derived tabulation of figures printed in a public national statistical report, attributed, not a copy of the report. Confirm with KNBS before this record is contributed to cdh-catalog. Required attribution: “This product was adapted from the Statistical Office of Kenya’s information, which is licensed under the KNBS Open License Agreement.”


[!WARNING] COUNTY ONLY. Volume XVI does not project below county - no sub-county name appears anywhere in the report - so this record stops at county. The KE-ENSO exposure tables (record kenya-flood-exposure-intersect) do carry sub-county figures for a projection year, and the way they get there is stated there in full: each sub-county’s share of its county is held fixed at the gridded 2020 distribution and the whole county is moved by its own percentage change from this table (pop_growth_county), with the enumerated census supplying the level. That means no sub-county-specific growth is represented; growth varies between counties (2025 factors span 1.03 to 1.15) but is uniform within one. Anyone wanting genuine sub-county differentials needs a source that produces them - this one does not. YEAR COVERAGE IS UNEVEN. The report’s annual panels cover 2020-2035; 2040 and 2045 appear only in the five-yearly milestone panel, so 2036-2039 and 2041-2044 are absent. TWO SOURCE DEFECTS, both handled and logged by the ingest rather than silently absorbed. (1) Busia 2030, age 80+, female reads 3,120 in the 2030-2035 panel against 5,799 in the two other panels that carry 2030; the printed row total (9,714) reconciles only with 5,799, so 5,799 is used. (2) Kiambu’s 2026-2030 panel labels its open-ended top age group “80-84” where every other panel says “80+”; it is relabelled “80+”, without which it would double-count against the overlapping panels. KNBS rounds each printed cell independently, so sums do not close exactly: age groups land within five people of the printed All Ages row, and the 47 counties sum to roughly 15 to 20 people below the national row in every year. The identical report is also hosted as …-Analytical-Report-on-Population-Projections-Vol-XVI.pdf (2024/05, 32.9 MB); its extracted text is identical to the 2023/09 upload used here.

text:
8.16 crop-vop-intld15: MapSPAM 2020 Adaptation Atlas, Sub-Saharan Africa
Category: Agri  |  Publishing State: authored  |  License: Open Data

8.16.1 Summary
Spatially disaggregated crop statistics for Sub-Saharan Africa: 42 crops across six production systems, harmonised to FAOSTAT country totals, as physical area, harvested area, production, yield and value of production. A regional adaptation of IFPRI’s MapSPAM 2020 built for the Africa Agriculture Adaptation Atlas, supplementing the global release with national and sub-national sources. This is the crop-production basis of the Atlas exposure chain: every crop value-of- production layer, and through them the hazard-exposure product, is distributed across these production shares.

Temporal Coverage: 2020
Spatial Resolution: sub-saharan-africa



8.16.2 Data Producers & Custodians

Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT - https://alliancebioversityciat.org/
International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) - https://www.ifpri.org/
Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (Peter Steward)



8.16.3 Scientific Caveats & Guidance

[!WARNING] NOT THE SAME DATASET AS THE HUB’S spam2020 RECORD, DESPITE THE NAME. That record describes IFPRI’s GLOBAL MapSPAM 2020 v2r2, licensed CC-BY-SA-4.0 and published as zarr. This one is the Atlas’s Sub-Saharan Africa adaptation, licensed CC-BY-4.0 and published as GeoTIFF. Different scope, different licence, different format, different DOI. Do not substitute one for the other, and note that the share-alike term on the global release does NOT reach the Atlas exposure chain, which consumes this product. THREE PROCESSING LEVELS, AND THEY ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE. raw holds the released CSVs, one file per variable and technology code (P_TA, P_TH, P_TI and so on). analysis-ready holds rasterised GeoTIFFs. atlas-harmonized holds the Atlas value-of-production layers derived from them. The VoP chain reads analysis-ready/variable=prod_t and writes into atlas-harmonized. FILE NAMING DIFFERS BETWEEN LEVELS. The irrigated system is irrigated under analysis-ready and irr under atlas-harmonized. Anything templating a path across both levels must special-case it; the token values below are given per level for that reason. CURRENCY BASIS IS A KNOWN TRAP. Several value-of-production variables coexist - vop_intld15, vop_usd2015, vop_nominal-usd15, vop_nominal-usd21 - and they are NOT interchangeable. A past mismatch between the crop and livestock currency bases produced roughly a sevenfold error in cattle exposure. Constant international dollars (vop_intld15) is the Atlas standard; check the livestock counterpart is on the same basis before combining. Tracked as hazards_prototype issue 30. THREE OBJECTS ARE PUBLISHED UNDER A MALFORMED KEY. Directly beneath region=ssa/ there are three parquet objects whose path reads processing=atlas-harmonizedvariable=<name>.parquet, missing the separator between the two hive fields: crop-livestock_all, vop_intld15-2021 and vop_nominal-usd-2021. They are not reachable by a hive-partitioned scan and should be republished or removed rather than left as a trap for the next reader.

8.17 livestock-vop: Gridded Livestock of the World (GLW4) Value of Production (Adaptation Atlas SSA)
Category: Agri  |  Publishing State: authored  |  License: Open Data

8.17.1 Summary
Spatial density distribution and economic value of production for major livestock species (cattle, sheep, goats, camels, pigs, chickens) across Sub-Saharan Africa. Based on FAO Gridded Livestock of the World v4 (GLW4 2020) downscaled to 1 km / 5-minute resolution, harmonised to FAOSTAT country production values and national livestock populations, expressed in constant 2015 international dollars (vop_intld15).

Temporal Coverage: 2020

Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (Peter Steward)



8.17.3 Scientific Caveats & Guidance

[!WARNING] Attribution: “Data provided by FAO Gridded Livestock of the World (GLW4) and compiled for the African Agriculture Adaptation Atlas (AAAA).” CURRENCY BASIS MUST REMAIN CONSTANT INTERNATIONAL DOLLARS (vop_intld15). Several value-of-production metrics coexist (nominal USD, constant 2015 international dollars). To avoid severe distortions when pairing livestock with MapSPAM crop VoP, both portfolios must be evaluated on the identical constant 2015 international dollar basis. Past unit mismatches produced ~7x errors in cattle exposure. DENSITY VS PIXEL COUNTS. GLW4-2020 layers represent per-km2 animal density (D-DA), not raw counts per grid cell. Spatial aggregation across county administrative polygons must weight by grid-cell land area (excluding open waterbodies). LIVESTOCK VULNERABILITY LAGS. Unlike annual field crops which fail within a single dry dekad, pastoral herds exhibit biological inertia: mortality, distress sales, and conception deficits lag rainfall anomalies by 6 to 12 months.

Audited subnational agricultural statistics from the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) National Agricultural Production Reports (NAPR 2023/24 and 2024/25 editions). Every number served from this dataset is parsed directly from published government PDF tables by deterministic code (_sources/napr_extract.py) and passed through an automated machine additivity gate. No language model reads, types, or imputes any numerical value. BLANK IS NOT ZERO. KNBS data is compiled from administrative expert-estimates. text:
8.20 kenya-market-prices-fews: Kenya Retail and Wholesale Market Prices (FEWS NET Data Warehouse)
Category: Markets  |  Publishing State: authored  |  License: Open Data

8.20.1 Summary
Staple and livestock market prices for Kenya from the FEWS NET Data Warehouse market price facts: 42 counties by market by product, 12 products, retail and wholesale, in Kenyan shillings, 2000 to 2026. Pulled through the FDW API. The price basis behind the Kenya ENSO Explorer’s market panel and behind the pastoral terms of trade shown there, which the Atlas derives rather than reads.

Temporal Coverage: 2000 to present (open-ended)
Spatial Resolution: kenya



8.20.2 Data Producers & Custodians

Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET), USAID - https://fews.net/
Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (Peter Steward)



8.20.3 Scientific Caveats & Guidance

[!WARNING] LICENCE IS A POLICY, NOT A CREATIVE COMMONS GRANT. FEWS NET provides data as a public service, managed under USAID’s policy on sharing Agency-funded data (ADS 579). Attribution is required, in the manner indicated in the metadata accompanying the data, prominently on any visual that uses it, with a link to the FEWS NET website, and without claiming or implying that FEWS NET endorses the use. FEWS NET disclaims liability and makes no guarantee of accuracy or completeness. THE CLAUSE THAT MATTERS FOR REDISTRIBUTION. FEWS NET states that “some data are provided by third parties, and may not be redistributed or reused without the consent of the original data provider, or may be subject to additional terms and conditions”, and instructs users to check the primary source’s own policy. Market price series are commonly collected by national agencies rather than by FEWS NET itself, so this clause is live for this dataset: reading the prices for analysis is unencumbered, republishing the series as an Atlas data product needs the originating agency identified first. Nothing derived from this is published by the Atlas today. TERMS OF TRADE IS OURS, NOT THEIRS. The pastoral terms of trade shown in the Explorer is computed here as goat price divided by maize price. It is not an NDMA figure and it is not published by FEWS NET in that form. It is a ratio, so it moves with either leg - a fall can mean cheaper livestock or dearer grain, which have opposite implications - and it should never be read as a price index. NOT NDMA. Kenya’s National Drought Management Authority publishes drought early warning bulletins carrying market prices and terms of trade, and an earlier version of the Atlas metadata wrongly named them as a source. No NDMA bulletin is fetched, parsed or mirrored anywhere. The NDMA bulletins remain a candidate source, held as a local draft record. COVERAGE IS UNEVEN. 42 of 47 counties appear, markets within a county vary, and a product is not quoted in every market in every month. Absence is a gap in market reporting, not a zero price.

text:
8.21 kenya-market-prices-kamis: Kenya Live-Animal Market Prices by Grade and Sex (MoALD KAMIS)
Category: Markets  |  Publishing State: draft  |  License: Open Data

8.21.1 Summary
Market-day livestock price quotes for Kenya from the Kilimo AgriMarkets Market Information System (KAMIS) of the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development (MoALD): cattle, sheep, goats and camels priced per head at named livestock markets in 45 counties, each quote carrying a breed (classification), a quality grade (1 to 3), the animal’s sex and the volume on offer, from May 2021 to the present. Harvested from the portal’s search export. The only verified open Kenyan source that prices camels and sheep and that records grade and sex, which the FEWS NET series behind the Kenya ENSO Explorer does not; it extends the explorer’s pastoral price panel from goats and cattle to all four pastoral species at market-day frequency.

Temporal Coverage: 2021-05-24 to present (open-ended)
Spatial Resolution: kenya



8.21.2 Data Producers & Custodians

Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development (MoALD), Kenya - https://kamis.kilimo.go.ke/
Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (Peter Steward)



8.21.3 Scientific Caveats & Guidance

[!WARNING] NO PUBLISHED LICENCE. The KAMIS portal (kamis.kilimo.go.ke) footer asserts “Copyright (c) KAMIS” and gives the Ministry’s contact (info@kilimo.go.ke, +254-20-2718870, Cathedral Road, Nairobi); it carries no licence statement and no terms of use, and the About page credits the National Agricultural and Rural Inclusive Growth Project (NARIGP) for the system. A copyright line without a licence is a reservation, not a grant. The Atlas reads the quotes for analysis and displays derived monthly medians; the market-day quotes are not republished to S3 or to the Climate Data Hub and no bulk download is offered until MoALD confirms terms of reuse. HOW THE PORTAL PAGES, AND WHY EARLIER COUNTS WERE WRONG. The HTML results table pages by an offset in the URL path (/site/market_search/), not by the page= query parameter, so one wide request returns only the first per_page rows. The Excel export honours per_page and returns a whole window in one file. The harvester pulls one export per species-year and checks the row count against the portal’s own pagination total; on 2026-10-23 that was 116,634 rows across the four species. WHOLESALE IS THE LIVESTOCK PRICE. 99.8 percent of live-animal quotes sit in the portal’s Wholesale column, which is the per-head price at the livestock market; the Retail column is essentially empty for animals. The explorer therefore serves these as wholesale prices, distinct from the FEWS NET retail goat and cattle series it already shows. THE 2021-05-24 BULK BACKFILL. The portal’s history starts on 2021-05-24, and that single date carries 11,079 quotes, about one tenth of the whole archive. It is the upload date of a backfill, not a market day. Those rows are kept in the market-day file with the flag launch_day_bulk and are excluded from the monthly medians. KAMIS cannot reach the 2011 or 2017 drought analogues; the FEWS NET series remains the long-run record. DIRTY ROWS ARE FLAGGED, NOT DROPPED. A county literally named test (345 quotes), 3,203 exact duplicate submissions, 67 non-positive prices and 591 order-of-magnitude outliers against the same market-day median are all present in the market-day file with a qc_flag, and absent from the monthly medians. County spellings are canonicalised to the 47-county key (Tana-River to Tana River, Homa-bay to Homa Bay, Muranga to Murang’a); the portal spelling is kept in county_raw. COVERAGE IS UNEVEN AND THINNING. Reporting peaked in 2022 (about 40,000 quotes) and fell to a few thousand a year by 2025; camel quotes stop at 2025-11-24. Absence of a market-month is a gap in reporting, not a zero price. Grade and breed are enumerator judgements with no published grading standard, so grade comparisons across markets are indicative only. NO COORDINATES. The portal names the market and county only; the file is plain parquet, not GeoParquet. OBFUSCATED DELIVERY, BY CHOICE. As a courtesy to the Ministry while reuse terms are sought, the market-day file is published to the explorer only as an AES-256-GCM container (market_prices_kamis.parquet.enc) that the explorer decrypts in the browser; the monthly medians it displays are derived aggregates. This stops casual download and crawling. It is not access control: a static page must hold whatever decrypts it, so a determined reader can recover the bytes. The plain file is not committed to the repository and no bulk download is offered.

Kenya Food Security Steering Group (KFSSG)
Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (Peter Steward)



8.22.3 Scientific Caveats & Guidance

[!WARNING] LICENCE CONFIRMED 2026-09-18, AND IT CONSTRAINS DOWNSTREAM USE. IPC states that all IPC results are licensed CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO. Two consequences that do not apply elsewhere in the Atlas stack: NON-COMMERCIAL, so IPC figures cannot travel into a commercially licensed or commercially used product; and SHARE-ALIKE, so any adapted work built on them must carry the same licence, which conflicts with the CC-BY-4.0 most Atlas products use. Citing IPC phases and linking out is unencumbered; folding them into a derived Atlas layer is not. The IPC Analysis Platform is hosted by FAO and governed by its terms of use. A PHASE IS A CLASSIFICATION, NOT A MEASUREMENT. Phases 1-5 come from an expert consensus process over converging evidence, so they are ordinal and are NOT comparable across analysis rounds in the way a measured index is: methodology, evidence base and analyst panel all change between rounds. Do not difference phases between rounds to derive a trend, and do not interpolate between analyses. Kenya analyses are conducted twice a year - long rains (July-August) and short rains (January-February) - and the IPC process is hosted within NDMA.

Category: Demographics  |  Publishing State: authored  |  License: Open Data

8.23.1 Summary

A federated record - the Adaptation Atlas reads these sheets but does not host or redistribute them.

Temporal Coverage: None
Spatial Resolution: kenya



8.23.2 Data Producers & Custodians

Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) - https://www.knbs.or.ke/
State Department for Gender and Affirmative Action, Ministry of Gender, Culture and Children Services
Council of Governors
UN Women (Women Count) - https://data.unwomen.org/women-count
SDGs Kenya Forum
Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (Peter Steward)



8.23.3 Scientific Caveats & Guidance

[!WARNING] LICENCE - AN EXPLICIT WORKING ASSUMPTION, NOT A GRANT. No party has published terms for these sheets. The Atlas treats them as open pending evidence otherwise, a decision taken by the data owner on 2026-09-18 and recorded here so it is visible rather than implied: LicenseRef-KE-Gov- Statistics-Assumed-Open means “no rights stated, treated as open”, NOT “the publishers granted an open licence”. Anyone relying on these figures commercially should confirm with the publishers first. The evidence behind the assumption follows. Every page of a sheet was read and the raw PDF scanned: there is NO copyright notice, NO “all rights reserved” and NO ISBN. That is materially better footing than the KNBS census projections (record kenya-population-knbs-projections, whose Volume XVI reserves rights in terms) - but absence of a notice is NOT a grant, and copyright subsists automatically. Worse, there is no single party whose terms could be pointed at: these are a six-way co-publication. The KNBS Open License Agreement does NOT reach them, being scoped to data published on the KNBS Open Data Platform, while these are PDFs on knbs.or.ke - the same gap already established for Volume XVI. UN Women co-publishes under the Women Count programme and normally releases CC-BY-3.0-IGO, which is a signal and not a statement. Settle with UN Women Kenya or the State Department for Gender before anything derived from these is published. EDITION. The October 2025 set, all 47 county sheets, uploaded to knbs.or.ke in April and May 2026. Not the 2019 ten-county pilot, and not a mix. A static cross-section, not an ongoing series. SIZE. The Atlas extraction yields 1,578 rows: 35 indicator series across 24 stable codes, long format, county level only. VINTAGE IS NOT UNIFORM AND IS NOT RECOVERABLE FROM THE SHEETS AS EXTRACTED. Indicators mix 2022 KDHS, 2019 census-derived figures and 2022 election results. The Atlas extraction strips any trailing year from indicator labels, so no per-indicator reference year survives in the derived table. Treating the whole table as “2022” is wrong for some indicators. BLANK IS NOT ZERO. The extraction serves a series only where at least 40 of 47 counties agree with the modal national value; non-matching county rows are dropped individually. So a served series can be silently missing up to seven counties, and a missing county-series is a parse or gate drop - NEVER an observed zero. Only 10 of 35 series reach all 47 counties; the worst is households with an elderly member at 40/47. Per-county row counts run 22-35. COVERAGE IS ASYMMETRIC WITHIN AN INDICATOR. One code can have 47 counties for male and 46 for female. Do not compute a sex ratio or a gender gap without checking both sides are present for that county. CHART-ONLY INDICATORS ARE ABSENT BY METHOD. Antenatal-visit and vaccination charts and internet usage are dropped by the gate. Their absence reflects the extraction, not the source. LABELS ARE NOT DEFINITIONS. The canonical label is the longest string seen across the 47 sheets and several remain truncated mid-sentence. Do not lift them into variable descriptions. COLUMN-ORDER FRAGILITY. Values are read Kenya-then-County from the printed header. A future edition that flips that header would swap every value silently; the coverage gate catches it only if the national column also becomes inconsistent.

title: 8  Controlled Vocabulary & Scientific Glossary
text:
9 Controlled Vocabulary & Scientific Glossary
This chapter provides standardized canonical definitions, abbreviations, mathematical notations, and institutional citations for all 84 domain terms across the Kenya ENSO Explorer platform. It establishes the controlled terminology required for interoperable subnational climate risk analytics.

title: 8  Controlled Vocabulary & Scientific Glossary
section: 9.1 Administrative & Geography
text:
9.1 Administrative & Geography

9.1.1 Arid and Semi-Arid Lands (ASAL)
The 23 designated arid and semi-arid counties of Kenya comprising over 80% of the national landmass, characterized by low and erratic rainfall, fragile rangeland ecosystems, and predominantly pastoralist livelihoods.
Mathematical Formulation / Metric: \[
\text{County Count} = 23 \text{ designated ASAL counties}
\]
Canonical Institutional / Literature Reference: Kenya Ministry of Devolution and ASALs.
Active in Platform Sections: 0.0, 1.0, 1.1, 4.3, 4.4


9.1.2 Common Operational Datasets - Administrative Boundaries (COD-AB)
The authoritative United Nations humanitarian GIS administrative boundary layers (ADM0 National, ADM1 County, ADM2 Sub-county) endorsed by UN OCHA and the Kenya Survey Department.
Mathematical Formulation / Metric: \[
Vector polygonal boundary layers with standardized P-codes
\]
Canonical Institutional / Literature Reference: UN OCHA Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX).
Active in Platform Sections: 1.0, 1.1, 3.4, 6.1


9.1.3 Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team Facilities (HOT-OSM)
Community-mapped geospatial vector points of health clinics, hospitals, and educational institutions in Kenya, validated for humanitarian disaster exposure modeling.
Mathematical Formulation / Metric: \[
Geospatial point feature layer
\]
Canonical Institutional / Literature Reference: Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team (HOT) Kenya Export.
Active in Platform Sections: 3.5, 4.5, 6.1


9.1.4 Kenya Power and Lighting Company Grid (KPLC)
National electrical transmission line infrastructure vector dataset used in the platform to evaluate power grid asset vulnerability to flood inundation.
Mathematical Formulation / Metric: \[
Vector line network (kV transmission lines)
\]
Canonical Institutional / Literature Reference: Kenya Power and Lighting Company GIS Repository.

section: 9.2 Climatology & Seasons
text:
9.2 Climatology & Seasons

9.2.1 Double Season Failure (Double Failure)
A production year in which both feeding seasons were Dry, that is a Dry/Dry consecutive sequence (OND of the preceding year and MAM of the same year both below −0.5 standard deviations of their own 1991–2020 climatology). Double failures remove the dry-season buffer of pasture, water and food stocks and are the historical signature of acute drought emergencies in Kenya.
Mathematical Formulation / Metric: \[
\text{DF}_Y = \mathbb{I}\left(z_{\text{OND},Y-1} < -0.5 \ \wedge\ z_{\text{MAM},Y} < -0.5\right)
\]
Canonical Institutional / Literature Reference: Kenya ENSO Explorer methods monograph, Figure 3.1B.
Active in Platform Sections: 3.1B


9.2.2 Long Rains (MAM)
The primary agricultural rainfall season across western, central, and northern Kenya, spanning the months of March, April, and May, driven by the northward migration of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ).
Mathematical Formulation / Metric: \[
R_{\text{MAM}} = \sum_{m \in \{\text{Mar, Apr, May}\}} R_m
\]
Canonical Institutional / Literature Reference: Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD) National Seasonal Calendar.
Active in Platform Sections: 0.0, 1.0, 2.1, 3.1, 3.1B, 4.1


9.2.3 Pastoral Boreal Summer Window (JJAS / JAS)
The dry season across eastern and southern pastoral rangelands (June–September) and the primary rainfall season in the western highlands and Lake Victoria basin.
Mathematical Formulation / Metric: \[
R_{\text{JJAS}} = \sum_{m \in \{\text{Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep}\}} R_m
\]
Canonical Institutional / Literature Reference: Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD) Regional Climatology.
Active in Platform Sections: 1.0, 3.1, 4.3


9.2.4 Short Rains (OND)
The secondary agricultural and pastoral rainfall season spanning October, November, and December, exhibiting the highest teleconnection sensitivity and predictive skill linked to Pacific ENSO and Indian Ocean Dipole dynamics.
Mathematical Formulation / Metric: \[
R_{\text{OND}} = \sum_{m \in \{\text{Oct, Nov, Dec}\}} R_m
\]
Canonical Institutional / Literature Reference: Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD) National Seasonal Calendar.
Active in Platform Sections: 0.0, 1.0, 2.1, 3.1, 3.1B, 4.1


9.2.5 WMO 1991–2020 Standard Normal Baseline (WMO Normal)
The canonical 30-year climatological reference period defined by the World Meteorological Organization for assessing contemporary climate anomalies and evaluating extreme frequencies.
Mathematical Formulation / Metric: \[
Calendar period 1991-01-01 through 2020-12-31 (30 complete historical years)
\]
Canonical Institutional / Literature Reference: WMO-No. 1203 (2017). WMO Guidelines on the Calculation of Climate Normals.
Active in Platform Sections: 0.0, 2.1, 3.1, 3.1B, 3.2, 6.1


9.2.6 Warm Dry Season Window (DJF)
The warm dry interval spanning December, January, and February, marked by crop maturation and harvesting in agricultural counties and grazing pressure in pastoral zones.
Mathematical Formulation / Metric: \[
R_{\text{DJF}} = R_{\text{Dec}} + R_{\text{Jan}} + R_{\text{Feb}}
\]
Canonical Institutional / Literature Reference: Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD).
Active in Platform Sections: 1.0, 3.1

section: 9.4 Economic & Valuation
text:
9.4 Economic & Valuation

9.4.1 Gross Value of Production (VOP)
The aggregate physical output of agricultural crops and livestock commodities valued at constant standardized gate prices, providing an uninflated metric of total agricultural capital at risk from climate extremes.
Mathematical Formulation / Metric: \[
\text{VOP}_{c} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} Q_{c,k} \times P_{k}^{\text{constant}}
\]
Canonical Institutional / Literature Reference: FAOSTAT Valuation Methodology / Beta Review Governance.
Active in Platform Sections: 1.2, 4.5


9.4.2 Standing Herd Capital (Herd Capital)
The replacement value of the live herd in a county, computed as head count times a capital-share adjustment for herd structure times the county sale price (0.75 of the mature sale price for cattle, goats and sheep; a species-specific herd-structure ratio for camels). It is a stock, distinct from the annual flow of offtake and milk, and is the quantity that drought mortality and distress sales erode.
Mathematical Formulation / Metric: \[
S_c = \sum_j H_{c,j}\, \kappa_j\, P^{\text{sale}}_{c,j}
\]
Canonical Institutional / Literature Reference: Behnke, R., & Muthami, D. (2011). The contribution of livestock to the Kenyan economy. IGAD LPI Working Paper 03-11.
Active in Platform Sections: 1.2

section: 9.5 Food Security & Vulnerability
text:
9.5 Food Security & Vulnerability

9.5.1 Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC)
A multi-partner standardized scale categorizing food insecurity severity into five distinct phases: Phase 1 (Minimal), Phase 2 (Stressed), Phase 3 (Crisis), Phase 4 (Emergency), and Phase 5 (Catastrophe/Famine).
Mathematical Formulation / Metric: \[
\text{Phase } \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}
\]
Canonical Institutional / Literature Reference: IPC Global Partners (2021). Integrated Food Security Phase Classification Technical Manual Version 3.1.
Active in Platform Sections: 4.6, 6.1


9.5.2 Reduced Coping Strategy Index (rCSI)
A standardized proxy measure of household food stress based on a weighted 5-question survey assessing behavioral adaptations taken by households experiencing food shortages over the past 7 days.
Mathematical Formulation / Metric: \[
\text{rCSI} = \sum_{i=1}^{5} w_i \times f_i, \quad w \in \{1, 1, 1, 2, 3\}
\]
Canonical Institutional / Literature Reference: Maxwell, D., et al. (2008). The Coping Strategies Index Field Methods Manual. CARE / WFP.
Active in Platform Sections: 4.6, 6.1
